title: The Unfurling Spiral Arms of NGC 3981
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 3981, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
celestial: NGC 3981 · constellation Crater · about 65 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Image processing: R. Colombari & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The outstretched arms of NGC 3981 seem to dissolve into space in this image. At the centre of this unbarred spiral galaxy, about 65 million light-years away in the constellation Crater, is a bright core that hosts a supermassive black hole, ringed by a disk of hot, young stars. Streams of dust thread through the spiral arms, along with further young stars.

The arms' irregular, stretched-out shape is probably the result of gravitational pull during an encounter with one of the galaxy's neighbours. NGC 3981 belongs to the NGC 4038 Group, which also includes the well-known interacting Antennae Galaxies.

That group, in turn, forms a small piece of the Virgo Supercluster, a vast assembly of galaxies to which the Milky Way also belongs. The picture was captured by the Dark Energy Camera (DECam), built by the Department of Energy, working on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (11.40 x 12.75 arcminutes) and distance (65 million light years), the frame spans roughly 216,000 × 241,000 light-years. Its light set out about 65 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Taken with DECam on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope through g and i filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
filters: 471 nm · Optical g (NSF Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope DECam)

understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, revealing the faint outer arms that fade into space.
